articles.title_orig: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The US Midterm Elections: Views From China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. midterm elections on November 3 were closely watched around the world as a way to gauge public support for the polarizing administration of Donald Trump. The verdict is in: the opposition Democratic Party won big, taking control of both houses of Congress with majorities Democrats haven’t enjoyed in years. Several states elected Democratic senators and governors for the first time in decades – in some cases, nearly a century .
Officially, of course, China won’t comment on the results of the election. That, as Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters on November 4, is “a domestic affair” of the United States. “China stands ready to continue working with the U.S. to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state,” Mao said.
In a speech delivered on election day, Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the United States, said , “A confident and composed China is committed to the steady, sound, and sustainable development of China-U.S. relations… China’s policy toward the United States remains consistent and stable.”
The first news readouts from Xinhua, China’s state news agency, were also terse, although the points of information they chose to include were telling. In one early article , for example, Xinhua did not mention the historic nature of Democratic Party wins, but instead quoted Trump’s social media post that “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The short, three-paragraph report also devoted the entire last paragraph to comments from a White House official, who predicted U.S. voters “will suffer from severe buyer’s remorse.”
Xinhua published a much longer analysis on November 4, highlighting four “unexpected” outcomes. This article delved into the massive scale of the Democratic victory, from the size of its new House majority to the flipping of Senate seats in traditionally safe Republican states like Texas, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina.
Rather than offering perspectives from Chinese analysts, Xinhua’s article extensively cited U.S. media, including this quote from the Wall Street Journal : “Rarely in American politics has a president traded away so much political support so quickly. The losses that Republicans suffered on Tuesday marked one of the most decisive repudiations of a president in modern history.”
Chinese state media had much less to say about the causes of the Republican defeat – again, Beijing’s official line being that this is an “internal affair” of the United States. However, Xinhua did cite the general thesis by U.S. analysts that economic dissatisfaction amid rising prices was the primary culprit. And those rising prices were exacerbated by the Trump administration’s decision to strike Iran. Xinhua published a whole article covering Vice President J.D. Vance’s post-election verdict that the war on Iran had cost the Republicans control of Congress.
One Xinhua report cited Iran’s Speaker of Parliament Mohammad Ghalibaf, who posted on X : “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.”
“What the Chinese public is most concerned about … is the impact of the U.S. midterm election results on the Iran war and Ukraine war,” Mu Chunshan, an independent political analysts based in Beijing, told The Diplomat via email. “They are less focused on the impact on China-U.S. relations. This is because Trump has consistently shown respect to China.”
If Democrats act to restrain Trump’s military operations in Iran, Mu said, it would be align “with China’s long-standing call for a peaceful resolution of the Iran nuclear issue.” He sees the election results as “conducive to China and other countries pushing for a negotiated resolution of the Iran nuclear issue and Strait [of Hormuz] security issues.”
That said, Chinese analysts are well aware of Congress’ limited control over foreign policy. In an pre-election analysis, South China Morning Post cited Zhao Zhijiang , a research assistant at the Beijing-based independent think tank Anbound, as predicting that “Diplomacy may become even more transactional. U.S. policy towards Russia, Iran, Europe and China could swing rapidly between heavy pressuring and partial bargaining.” In other words, China is bracing for impact as a notoriously mercurial leader feels increased political pressure at home.
Diao Daming, an international relations professor at Renmin University in Beijing, told SCMP Trump might become more “legacy-driven” in his pursuit of foreign policy.  “On the other hand, in areas he believes he can control or achieve results quickly, he may also take some risky actions,” Diao said.
With a Trump-Xi summit looming later this month, China will be one of the first to get a feel for how the midterm defeat impacts Trump’s foreign policy style. China is hosting the APEC Leaders’ Meeting from November 18-19, with Trump expected to attend. Beside yet another summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping – the third in 2026 alone – there has been much discussion of other potential sideline meetings, including a possible China-Russia-U.S. trilateral.
China had its own reasons to be skeptical about hosting such a meeting . After the midterm outcomes, which will likely result in increased congressional support for Ukraine, there’s even less reason for Beijing to look positively on the prospects of a Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.
“At the APEC summit, if China, the US and Russia hold a trilateral summit, there is a high probability that the Ukraine war will not be discussed, because the midterm results make it harder for Trump to pressure Ukraine into accepting a ‘land-for-peace’ plan.” Mu said. “For China, discussing this is meaningless. Any peace plan must indeed fully take into account the views of Ukraine and Europe. This should be similar to the views of the new U.S. Congress.”
Also with the APEC summit in mind, Chinese policymakers will want to see if Trump is willing to strike a bargain to secure quick economic gains, given U.S. voter anger over the cost of living. There is also hope that a Democratic Congress would do more to push back on Trump’s use of tariffs – a tool that typically belongs to the legislative branch, not the executive, under the U.S. system of government.
“If the Democrats can restrain Trump’s impulses to China and other countries in the areas of tariffs and trade, that would be better for China-U.S. relations,” Mu said.
But few in China expect a Democratic-majority Congress to look too much different. “Structural contradictions exist in China-U.S. relations, and both the two parties share negative views on China, for example on national security or high-tech competition,” Mu noted. “These will not change in any particular way due to the outcome of the midterms.”
More broadly, Chinese analysts largely took the U.S. election results as evidence for already-held assumptions about a crumbling U.S. political system. Xinhua’s own original reporting , including on-the-street interviews with voters, portrayed a sense of pessimism and despair. Nearly all the quotes were from voters who expressed doubt that anything would change, regardless of who is in power. One sample: “I have no confidence in any politician, and I don’t think they will focus on what is right for us.”
That was a far cry from the palpable sense of optimism emanating from the Democratic Party as the election results rolled in. But it does fit nearly with China’s preferred thesis that the United States is locked into an irreversible decline.
And whatever Beijing may say about the election being the United States’ “domestic affair,” it will not be lost on Chinese leaders that an unpopular war far from home, and its economic consequences, resulted in severe political punishment for the ruling party. That will factor in to China’s ongoing calculations about what the Iran-U.S. war might imply about Americans’ appetite for intervention in a Taiwan crisis.

articles.content_orig:
As coalition negotiations loom and allegations of foreign election interference emerge, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Tel Aviv, Israel.
TEL AVIV, Israel - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition remained well short of a parliamentary majority Thursday as newly counted ballots showed a dramatic surge in support for Arab parties, potentially giving the opposition enough votes to challenge his control of parliament.
With 93.8% of ballots counted as of 4 a.m. ET Thursday (10 a.m. local time in Israel), including votes from the double-envelope count, Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc was projected to win 53 seats in Israel's 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. The two predominantly Arab parties were projected to secure a combined 19 seats, bringing the potential anti-Netanyahu parliamentary majority to 67.
The updated figures showed Netanyahu's Likud remaining the largest individual party with 26 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar party with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad party with 12. The figures remain preliminary.
NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on Oct. 20, 2026. (Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images)
The results leave neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with the 61 seats required to form a government independently, raising the prospect of difficult coalition negotiations or another election.
The biggest shift came from Israel's Arab voters, whose turnout surged compared with previous elections, potentially reshaping the country's political balance.
Arab voter participation reached approximately 80%, compared with 53.2% in the 2022 election, according to the Israel Democracy Institute . The 2026 figure remains preliminary.
The Joint List was projected to win 11 seats, while Ra'am was projected to secure eight. Together, their 19 seats would nearly double the Arab parties' representation from the 10 seats they won in 2022.
Overall voter turnout reached 77.7% by the official 10 p.m. closing time on election night, the highest level at that hour since 1999, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee.
The increased Arab participation could prove decisive in determining the next government's composition. Although Eisenkot and several other opposition leaders ruled out including Arab parties in their governing coalition during the campaign, their parliamentary support could allow the opposition to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, and gain greater control over the legislative agenda even before a new government is formed.
IRAN IS TRYING TO ‘CREATE A ROT FROM WITHIN’ THROUGH ‘INFORMATION WARFARE,’ ANALYST WARNS
Posters of Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu are displayed on billboards ahead of the Knesset elections, in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 25, 2026. (Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images)
The political stakes intensified Thursday following a Channel 12 report alleging that substantial sums originating in Qatar may have been transferred to influence voter participation in Arab communities.
According to N12, some of the funds allegedly traveled through financial channels previously used to transfer money to terrorist organizations , including currency exchanges.
The allegations have not been independently substantiated, and investigators have yet to establish whether foreign financing occurred or whether election-related crimes were committed.
Channel 12 reported that Shin Bet Director David Zini presented intelligence concerning suspected foreign interference to Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, prompting the judge to order an investigation.
In a letter published by N12 , Sohlberg instructed the domestic security agency to investigate the allegations and identify evidence that could either substantiate or disprove them. He requested findings within one week, citing the limited time available during the election count.
The judge's letter did not publicly identify Qatar as the suspected foreign actor. That identification came from N12's reporting.
Qatar strongly denied the allegations Thursday, accusing Israeli politicians of attempting to drag the Gulf nation into Israel's domestic political disputes following the election.
"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr. Majed Al-Ansari wrote on X.
Al-Ansari accused Israeli politicians and their allies in the media of launching a "disinformation campaign," saying Qatar had been accused of financing Netanyahu, the Israeli left and now Arab voters.
"If these claims were to be believed, Qatar would apparently own all of Israel," he wrote. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians," Al-Ansari added, insisting that Qatar had no involvement in Israel's electoral process and would continue its diplomatic and humanitarian efforts in the region.
Acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne also rejected the allegations in a letter to Yesh Atid MK Vladimir Beliak, who sits on the committee. "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Israel's Shin Bet security agency clarified Thursday that the intelligence behind the investigation was gathered independently and did not originate from any political party. It said no one outside the agency, except Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, had access to the information before the election ended.
The agency stressed that the investigation remains ongoing and warned against drawing premature conclusions.
The investigation "does not cast aspersions on or accuse an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and lawfully," the Shin Bet said in a statement translated from Hebrew.
The agency also confirmed that Shin Bet Director David Zini had briefed Netanyahu, Eisenkot and opposition leader Yair Lapid on the allegations, with Sohlberg's approval.

But the allegations have already become part of the political confrontation over whether opposition parties should cooperate with Arab lawmakers.
Netanyahu and Likud had  challenged the legitimacy of the Arab parties' electoral gains. On Wednesday, before the latest Qatari allegations emerged, Likud accused Arab parties of stealing the election through alleged voter fraud, accusations that had not been substantiated.
In a statement Thursday, Likud argued that the suspected foreign interference made cooperation with the Arab parties unacceptable.
"After it became clear that foreign actors attempted to take control of the Knesset, it is obvious that no Zionist party must cooperate with Ra'am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker using votes bought with cash, or establish a government dangerous to Israel," the party said.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: AI Stocks Under Pressure While Dow Futures Rise — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: AI Stocks Under Pressure While Dow Futures Rise — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite plummeted on Thursday, a day after a massive rally on the heels of Democrats' midterm wins , as investors rotated away from technology stocks for another day.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq declined 3.1%, while the S&P 500 was down 1.7%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 391 points, or 0.8%.
Stocks related to the artificial intelligence trade — particularly those linked to the chips industry and data centers — slid for a second day. Investors fear that a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress as well as victories in key gubernatorial races could spell more regulation of the AI buildout across the country.
Chipmakers Broadcom and Nvidia each fell 5% Thursday, while others such as software stock Oracle declined close to 5%. Additionally, Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX dropped 9% and 7%, respectively. Another chip stock Qualcomm reported earnings that beat estimates , but the stock dropped 9% on a weaker-than-expected earnings outlook.
Shares of neocloud companies retreated, with CoreWeave losing 9%, Nebius losing 13% and Iren shedding 11%, amid those worries about a backlash to the industry in light of the election results in various states.
On the positive side, AppLovin — the AI-powered advertising company — surged 32% after delivering better-than-expected results and issuing guidance that beat estimates.
Trading on Wednesday showed investors adjusting to midterm results, which showed Democrats securing comfortable majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. The Dow jumped more than 1,500 points to notch its best day since April 2025, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite popped more than 1% each.
Jordan Watson, a portfolio manager at Tandem Investment Advisors, said the big rally and the rotation away from artificial intelligence names could be temporary.
"We may be headed for more volatility as investors digest the election results and potential policy implications," he said. "I wouldn't view [Wednesday's equity trading] as an all-clear signal, but rather a call for some sanity around the amount of capital being poured into the AI infrastructure build-out and whether those investments will generate the returns investors expect."
U.S. crude oil — which tumbled below $90 per barrel on Wednesday as investors anticipated that the Democratic Party may use their newfound leverage to pressure President Donald Trump into ending the Iran war — reversed course Thursday. West Texas Intermediate futures were last up more than 1% to just below $90 a barrel, while Brent crude futures gained more than 2% to around $97.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average began Thursday's session in the green.
The blue-chip Dow added 334 points, or 0.6%, just after the opening bell. The S&P 500 dipped 0.1%, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 0.7%.
Jobless claims slipped further last week, hovering around levels not seen since the late 1960s, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
Initial filings for unemployment claims totaled a seasonally adjusted 189,000 for the week ended Oct. 31, down 6,000 from the prior period and below the Dow Jones consensus estimate for 197,000. The total tied for the lowest since July, which was the bottom going back to September 1969.
Continuing claims, which run a week behind, rose 23,000 to 1.72 million.
Productivity posted a stronger-than-expected jump in the third quarter while the portion of output that showed up in worker pay hit a record low, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday.
Nonfarm business sector productivity surged 3.6% for the period, up from 2.1% in the second quarter and well ahead of the Dow Jones consensus estimate for 2.9%. Compensation less productivity, a metric known as unit labor costs, contracted 0.7%.
At the the same, the percentage of output that goes to workers in the form of compensation, known as the labor share, slipped further to 53%, the lowest in a data series that dates back to 1947.
Check out the companies making headlines before the bell:
The stock market skyrocketed on Wednesday on the heels of a decisive sweep for Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections . But that was not necessarily the only driver of the climb.
"President Trump's acknowledgement of the Democrats' victory in the midterms and his expressed openness to collaborating with the opposition have helped markets to rally on hopes that contestation of the results and more adverse polarization can be avoided," said Thomas Hempell, Generali Investments senior economist.
Trump told The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal overnight Tuesday that he accepted the results and would work with Democrats. Those headlines coincided with a rebound in stock market futures.
Read the full story here .
Wendy's shares were down slightly after the fast food chain on Thursday rejected a a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a Trian Fund Management-led group.
The group late last month offered $7.35 per share in cash to take Wendy's private.
The U.S. midterms could widen the AI divide: tighter data center rules may reward tech giants with capacity in hand and squeeze debt-funded companies trying to catch up.
Democratic victories in key gubernatorial races raised the prospect of tougher scrutiny for data center projects, adding to investor concerns about how quickly new capacity can be built and financed.
OpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday, two days after voters at the polls roundly rejected the rapid expansion of AI.
The FTSE 100 touched a three-month high on Thursday morning.
The U.K.'s blue-chip index rose as much as 119 points to 10,948, up more than 1.1% in early trading and reaching its highest level since Aug 7.  The index was last seen 0.86% higher.
The rise comes as traders await the Bank of England's latest interest rate decision, due later Thursday. The market expects the central bank's rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee to raise rates by 25 basis points to 4% from 3.75% — its first hike in more than three years.
Shares in British lenders moved higher ahead of the BoE's decision, due at 12:00 p.m. in London (7:00 a.m. E.T.). Barclays was up 2.2%, while Lloyds Banking Group added 1.9% and NatWest was 1.4% higher.
Sterling was up almost 0.1% against the dollar at $1.3482.
German defense giant Rheinmetall cut its full-year guidance late Wednesday, citing delays to military contracts and ammunition deliveries, sending shares down as much as 16% in early trading.
It marks the company's second outlook cut since August, when Germany scrapped plans to build warships in what would have been Rheinmetall's biggest order since World War II. The defense company now expects sales to rise to around 13.2 billion euros ($14.9 billion) in 2026, down from a prior outlook range of between 13.7 billion and 14.2 billion euros. It is expected to have an operating margin of around 18.5%, down from the previously expected 19%.
Rheinmetall said it's revising its 2026 guidance due to delays in the German military's Arminius Boxer project, now expected to be commissioned next year, and setbacks in artillery ammunition acceptance testing.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was up 0.48% shortly after 8:05 a.m. in London (3:05 a.m. in E.T.), as the continent's major bourses and sectors opened the day in the green.
Basic resources led gains, rising 2.51%, followed by autos and parts, which rose 2.05%. Travel and leisure stocks added 1.76%. Oil and gas reversed by 1.84%.
In Paris, France's CAC 40 was up 1.08%, as the U.K. FTSE 100 advanced 1.05% in London. In Milan, the Italian FTSE MIB was up almost 0.1%, and Germany's DAX added 0.16% in Frankfurt.

articles.title_orig: Flight bomb threats live: Multiple planes in Europe diverted for second time in a week
articles.title_zh: Flight bomb threats live: Multiple planes in Europe diverted for second time in a week
articles.content_orig:
• Bomb threats forced the diversion of more than a dozen flights across Europe on Thursday, the latest in a string of incidents disrupting airspace. Several authorities have said no devices have been found.
• Four of the flight diversions were in the Czech Republic. The bomb threats were made in an anonymous email and other airports received the email too, a representative of the Václav Havel Airport in Prague told CNN .
• A company linked to Rome’s airport received an email from a group purporting to be anti-feminist and calling itself the Male State that claimed there were bombs on two flights. But it is unconfirmed who was behind the wave of threats and the EU says it is too early to say they are linked.
Matthew Bojarsky’s LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Paris was taxiing to the runway when the pilot announced it had been cancelled for safety reasons.
Passengers were told the plane would wait at the end of the runway for “some officers,” he told CNN, after posting a video on X that shows men in military fatigues outside the plane.
Eventually the flight, one of more than a dozen to face bomb threats on Thursday,  was continued on a different plane.
“We were moved into a hall, then waited for four hours,” Bojarsky said. “We got the information from the news, the pilot said it was ‘safety protocol’.”
Officials at the Madrid-Barajas Airport in Spain’s capital received a “bomb threat” naming three flights on Thursday, airport operator AENA said.
Law enforcement teams carried out an assessment “and the relevant security checks” and found nothing on board, a spokesperson for AENA told CNN.
An anti-feminist group calling itself “The Male State” emailed bomb threats to a logistics company working with Rome Fiumicino Airport on Thursday naming two flights bound for the Italian capital.
The email, first published by CNN Affiliate SkyTG24, made the false claim that “explosive devices” had been placed on two flights – one from Helsinki and another from Dublin. A spokesperson for the airport confirmed to CNN the screenshot was authentic.
“You’re all complicit in a criminal plot, we want to annihilate you for this,” the memo read in Italian. “We, the fighters of the Male State, with our actions will leave a mark on history. Your feminist regime will never forget it.”
Earlier on Thursday , Italian air force fighter jets escorted the Finnair flight from Helsinki safely into Rome airport. A second flight from Dublin to Rome, operated by the Irish airline, Aer Lingus, was diverted to Normandy, northern France.
The email went to Aviapartner, a Belgium-based logistics company providing luggage services to the Rome airport.
The email alias appeared to be linked to the municipality of the Colombian capital Bogotá, whose mayor Luis Fernando Galan told CNN his team was working to establish what happened.
“It could be the account was hacked, we’ve had several of them before,” Galan told CNN.
Aviapartner declined to comment to CNN.
The EU transport commissioner said it is “too early” to determine whether the bomb threats that caused several flights to be diverted and others escorted to their scheduled destination across Europe this week are connected.
“It is too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked,” Apostolos Tzitzikostas said in a statement released Thursday, “National investigations remain ongoing.”
The commissioner said that the situation is being closely monitored, and that the department is “in contact with the affected member states and the European Aviation Safety Agency.”
“The EU-level information sharing mechanism has been activated related to aviation security,” it added.
The commissioner said any threat against civilians is “unacceptable,” and said all relevant bodies have been liaising to ensure aviation safety and security is not compromised.
While no explosive devices have yet been found following bomb threats, the motivation behind the reports remains unclear.
The UK’s transport minister says the bomb threats that have caused several flights to be diverted and others escorted to their destinations are a “malicious hoax.”
Speaking to British media, Heidi Alexander said that the disrupted flights had triggered “established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats, and that’s what these threats have been.”
While the minister insisted that the British government is taking the threats seriously, she added “we understand these have been malicious hoax threats.”
At least 14 flights have been impacted by the threats Thursday. No explosives have yet been found.
Bulgaria’s transport authorities are the latest to confirm that their inspections found no issues on any of the three aircraft that were the subject of this morning’s bomb threats.
Two Ryanair flights to Sofia from Madrid and Copenhagen respectively landed safely at their destination after the bomb threats.
Another Ryanair flight from London was diverted to Plovdiv, southeast of the capital, following a threat.
“Upon landing, the necessary inspections were carried out in accordance with the applicable procedures and no issues were identified,” a spokesperson for Bulgaria’s transport ministry told CNN Thursday.
Both airports are operating as normal and the airline arranged transportation to Sofia from Plovdiv for diverted passengers.
A representative of the Václav Havel Airport in Prague told CNN the threats it received about bombs being placed on four flights were made in an anonymous email.
A Czech Police spokesperson told CNN the email was addressed to the airport, adding that similar emails were sent to other airports in Europe.
The Prague airport immediately contacted emergency services and convened a meeting of its crisis committee.
Neither the airport representative nor the police said which language the email was written in.
In another incident, almost 200 passengers were evacuated from a Wizz Air flight after it landed safely in Bucharest, Romania, Thursday morning local time following a bomb threat, bringing the total to at least 14.
Romania’s intelligence agency said the aircraft, which departed from Milan, has been checked and no explosives found, Reuters reported.
Two planes from European cities were diverted to Malpensa Airport in Milan, in Italy on Thursday following bomb threats, according to airport officials.
Italian border police were carrying out “bomb checks” on both planes, the airport said in a statement. One Aegean Airlines flight had set off from Thessaloniki, northern Greece, while the other was a Ryanair flight from the city of Porto, northern Portugal.
The Czech National Center against Terrorism, Extremism and Cybercrime, a specialized unit of the Czech Police, is taking over the investigation into the threats made against four airplanes headed to Prague.
Czech authorities are in contact with their international partners, Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said on X.
A plane rerouted a flight from Dublin to Rome following a bomb threat is now at the Evreux air base in Normandy.
The plane “landed safely,” according to the Irish carrier, Aer Lingus.
About 151 passengers and six crew members were “being moved to safety” following the “bomb threat,” the French prime minister’s office said.
There’s no word yet whether there was a bomb on board but other national authorities say the threats they received were hoaxes.
Much is unknown about the latest threats to flights - no one claimed responsibility for the alerts earlier this week and no one has claimed Thursday’s threats either.
But, coming off the back of hackers targeting supermarket fridges, experts say such attacks could serve multiple purposes, from causing disruption to testing authorities’ response.
“These aviation threats are also occurring in the same period as cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe,” said Eliran Almog, CEO of aviation cybersecurity firm Cyviation.

Chip stocks sank on Thursday, extending declines from the prior session. Despite a broader market rally on Wednesday following Democrats' midterm election victory, semiconductor stocks moved lower amid the threat that stricter regulation could slow data center construction.
Semiconductor stocks, which drove the AI trade higher this year, have been volatile since the summer. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) fell by more than 5% in early trading, trimming the index's year-to-date gains to roughly 35%.
The declines were led by Qualcomm ( QCOM ), which issued an underwhelming profit forecast , signaling that higher-cost components are weighing on the smartphone processor maker.
Shares of Arm Holdings ( ARM ) also fell after the chip designer issued revenue guidance that, while slightly above consensus, failed to impress investors who priced in a higher range amid the AI boom.
Micron Technology ( MU ) stock also declined after the memory chipmaker paused plans for a Taiwanese plant due to labor disputes. Sandisk ( SDNK ) slid 6%, extending declines from 7% in the prior session.
SK Hynix ( SKHY ) was also trading lower in premarket trading after shares of the South Korean memory maker tumbled overseas, alongside Samsung Electronics ( 005930.K S ).
At the same time, shares of US chipmaker Intel ( INTC ) declined nearly 5%, while AMD ( AMD ) plunged 9%. Nvidia ( NVDA ) also extended declines from the prior session.

The Signature 27 comes with true flagship specs — and a price that has RAMageddon written all over it.
Motorola is trying something it hasn’t attempted in the modern smartphone era: to make an all-out flagship slab-style phone.
Previous high-end Edge devices never quite hit the mark , and lacked features that would put it in the highest flagship tiers. The company has had plenty of success with its Razr clamshell foldables, leaning on brand nostalgia and daring to make phones that actually look good. But it’s trying something different with its new Signature line , which until now hasn’t been available in the US. The Signature 27 goes a step further toward premium, daring to take on the likes of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. Motorola is leaning into a luxury aesthetic, offering a stacked feature set — with an equally luxurious $1,599 price tag.
It’s a lot to ask for a starting price, but it does get you 512GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, the same as the S26 Ultra’s $1,599, 512GB variant. Samsung does offer a cheaper 256GB configuration for $1,399, though.
We got our first look at the Signature 27 when Motorola previewed it earlier this year , revealing that it would use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. The company dropped a few other details, too, like Bang & Olufsen-designed audio, 50-megapixel and 200-megapixel telephoto cameras, and two Pantone color options. Today’s full announcement fills in the gaps. It will come with a 7,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, a 6.8-inch tandem OLED screen, IP68/IP69 ratings for full dust and water resistance, and 12GB of RAM. The Signature 27 will also support the privacy-focused GrapheneOS — a first for Motorola, and for a mainstream phone sold in the US, for that matter.
It’s hard to find fault with the 27’s feature set, aside from the lack of built-in Qi2 magnets, which is a bummer. The tandem OLED display uses two light-emitting panels to reach a peak brightness of 12,000 nits. The more battery efficient dual-layer might mean that the phone can reach its highest brightness setting without drawing too much power and overheating the phone, but we’ll want to see if that bears out in practice.
The camera array features a 50-megapixel Sony Lytia L910 sensor with LOFIC technology , meaning it should deliver plenty of dynamic range. In addition to a 3x 200-megapixel camera and a 50-megapixel ultrawide, there’s also an Event Vision Sensor, or EVS. It’s designed to identify movement on a pixel level, which Motorola says will help “capture fast-moving subjects with greater clarity and precision.”
That Bang & Olufsen audio system includes a redesigned speaker architecture for sound that’s “meant to be felt, not just heard,” according to Motorola’s press release. That’d be quite a feat to pull off with a smartphone audio system and I’m not holding my breath. Elsewhere, the Signature 27 offers up to 90W wired charging and up to 50W wireless charging — though you’ll need to use Motorola’s proprietary wireless charger. But in better news, Motorola is promising seven years of OS upgrades for the Signature 27, putting it right up there with the best support policies from Samsung and Google.
Maybe it’s a case of unlucky timing that Motorola decided to go toe-to-toe with Samsung’s premium flagship just as we started gearing up for RAMageddon: Year Two. Maybe in a few years’ time every flagship phone will cost well over $1,000. But right now, $1.600 is a steep hill to ask people to climb, and the Signature 27 will need to come up with more than just an impressive spec sheet.
And just to prove a point, Motorola is also announcing some updates to its wider ecosystem, too. The new Moto Watch Fit 27 claims up to 12 days of battery life, and the Moto Buds 27 offer Bose ANC with IP57 ratings for both the buds and the case. Motorola isn’t announcing pricing or an exact release date for either in the US, only that they’ll be available in the coming months. Both will arrive in the coming “weeks” in Europe and the UK, where the watch will start at £99.99 (about $134 US) and the buds will cost £179.99 (about $242).
Pre-sales for the Signature 27 start on November 19th in the US; the phone goes on sale November 26th.

articles.title_orig: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.title_zh: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.content_orig:
French riot police fired tear gas and charged a group of protesters in the French city of Lyon on Thursday as demonstrations took place across the country in a renewed challenge to President Emmanuel Macron after weeks of unrest.
Some of the protesters were seen shouting anti-police slogans and some were dressed all in black, with face coverings.
The Interior Ministry said police in Lyon had been confronted by several hundred hardcore protesters and that the violence had been contained, although tensions remained high.
Riot police in Lyon detain protesters during a demonstration for higher wages and in support of the high school protest movement on Thursday. (Laurent Cipriani/The Associated Press)
The nationwide protests and a strike by public workers, called by trade unions and backed by student groups, come after demonstrations over living costs, public services and education triggered the worst civil unrest France has seen in years.
The unrest comes only five months before a presidential election, which could pit far-right candidate Marine Le Pen against hard-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon in a second-round runoff. Macron, who is serving his second term and is unpopular, cannot run again.
The Interior Ministry said people throwing fireworks had caused a fire at a high school near the city of Toulouse in the southwest on Thursday morning, forcing pupils and staff to evacuate the building while firefighters doused the flames.
"This criminal behavior is an absolute scandal," said Education Minister Edouard Geffray on X.
French high school students and other demonstrators had earlier faced off against riot police in Paris as they blocked a street with rubbish bins on Thursday morning.
A protester dressed as the superhero Deadpool rides a toy unicorn during the Thursday demonstration in Lyon. (Laurent Cipriani/The Associated Press)
While the demonstrations in Lyon and other cities, including Marseille and Nantes, began in the morning, the main protest in Paris was only scheduled to start at 2 p.m. local time,.
The Eiffel Tower was shut on Thursday because of the strike.
"The government tried to block the demonstrations. The demonstrations are bigger than ever," Sophie Binet, head of the CGT trade union, told reporters. She estimated that some 250,000 people were demonstrating across France.
"High school students, pensioners, students, workers, all together. Unity wins," read one banner at the protest in Lyon.
"Our pay has not kept up with inflation," said Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter who was joining the protest in Paris.
"What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced," he said, referring to wildfires caused earlier this year by intense heat waves.
Authorities had sought to lower tensions after riots and looting on Oct. 17 caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops and public buildings across the country and fuelling criticism of Macron's handling of the crisis.
A car burns during a demonstration in Lyon. (Laurent Cipriani/The Associated Press)
Around 70,000 police were on duty nationwide, a comparable figure to recent weekends. The French government has defended police tactics while saying any abuses would be investigated.
The Education Ministry said just over 15 per cent of French teaching staff had joined the strike.
The movement began in September with a protest over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris and spread nationwide. It drew students demanding more education funding and workers seeking better pensions and help with soaring fuel prices and other costs.
The rallies come as the campaign to succeed Macron as president next May heats up, with political parties seeking to capitalize on the movement. Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the favourite to win.

articles.title_orig: Bank of England Raises Rates as Iran War Pushes Up Prices
articles.title_zh: Bank of England Raises Rates as Iran War Pushes Up Prices
articles.content_orig:
The Bank of England announced its first interest rate hike in over three years on Thursday, raising its key rate by 25 basis points to 4%.
The widely anticipated move marked the bank's first hike since Aug. 2023, and made it the last major central bank to embark on a tightening cycle since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran eight months ago.
The majority of the bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted for the quarter-point hike, with the motion passing by 8 votes to 1. The dissenting member voted to raise the bank's key interest rate by 50 basis points to 4.25%.
"The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month," the MPC said in a statement Thursday. "Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level."
Policymakers said they now expected U.K. inflation to rise to "about 5%" by the middle of 2027.
"It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation," they said.
Ahead of the decision being announced, markets had been pricing in more than a 99% chance of a rate hike, according to LSEG data. Traders were also pricing in a one-in-four chance of a further hike in December.
Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said in the November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside."
"Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics," he said.
Data released earlier this month showed that the U.K.'s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.5% in September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels.
As a net energy importer, the U.K. is particularly vulnerable to external energy shocks — such as the one caused this year by the Iran war.
The MPC's most hawkish member, Catherine L Mann, said she had voted for greater tightening than her peers because research pointed to "non-linear inflation risks."
"My recent votes to increase Bank Rate by 25 basis points represented a 'down payment' to lean against second-round effects, reinforce credibility, and uphold 'good policy'," she said in comments published in the MPC's policy statement.
"The economy has crossed the estimated statistical threshold into a high inflation-tight labour market regime where the asymmetric behavioural responses of households and firms support more robust second-round effects," Mann added. "A different research approach estimates that the economy may well have breached the policy credibility threshold, which worsens the policy trade-off... From a risk management and credibility perspective, a 50-basis point hike in Bank Rate is 'good policy'."
Yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, had been rising before the policy announcement and continued to edge higher after the Bank of England's update. The yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt was last seen 2 basis points higher at 5.1546%, while the 2-year gilt yield rose by 4 basis points to trade at 4.782%.
The British pound , which hit a post-Brexit high on Wednesday, was flat against both the U.S. dollar and the euro on Thursday afternoon.
Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JPMorgan Personal Investing, said in a note on Thursday that the November hike was "hugely symbolic."
"This is a 180-degree turn from the start of the year when many believed interest rates would come down as UK inflation had been mostly tamed," he said.
"The path ahead remains uncertain with much depending not only on how oil trades but also on natural gas prices which have risen sharply over the past few months. Worryingly, there are tentative signs of second round inflation effects in the UK economy as we have seen an acceleration in goods and services inflation. The Bank will be wary of this but also conscious of being too aggressive with rate hikes which could stunt the positive UK economic growth we've seen of late."

articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects takeover proposal from Nelson Peltz’s Trian
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects takeover proposal from Nelson Peltz’s Trian
articles.content_orig:
Wendy's on Thursday said it is rejecting a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management.
The group offered $7.35 per share in cash on Oct. 28 to take the struggling burger chain private . In addition to Trian, it included investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.
In February, Wendy's board formed a committee of independent directors to assess any potential bid from Trian in response to a regulatory filing from the firm. The committee found that the proposal "substantially undervalues" Wendy's and does not reflect potential gains from the chain's ongoing turnaround strategy, the company said in a press release Thursday.
"Our confidence rests firmly in [CEO] Bob Wright's proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds," Art Winkleblack, Wendy's board chair and a member of the independent committee, said in a statement.
Trian declined to comment on Wendy's decision.
To stave off a hostile takeover, Wendy's has adopted a shareholder rights plan — or poison pill — with a one-year duration, as of Wednesday, the company said. Wendy's added that the investor group led by Trian rejected an offer from Wendy's for a standstill agreement that would have paused additional share purchases, adding to Wendy's decision to use a poison pill.
The rejection is the latest in the long-running saga between Peltz and the burger chain, which dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago. A Peltz firm has even owned Wendy's before. In 2008, his company Triarc, which also owned Arby's, bought Wendy's in a $2.3 billion deal. It later sold Arby's, turning Wendy's into a stand-alone company again.
In 2024, Wendy's named Peltz as chairman emeritus after he spent 17 years on the company's board. Trian executive Peter May and Peltz's son, Bradley, still sit on Wendy's board.
Wendy's also reported its third-quarter results on Thursday. Its same-store sales declined for the seventh straight quarter. However, its quarterly earnings and revenue topped Wall Street's expectations.
Shares of Wendy's fell less than 1% in morning trading. The takeover offer had lifted the stock, which has lost about 60% of its value over the last three years.
Wendy's is not the only restaurant chain that has found itself in the crosshairs of activist investors recently. Applebee's owner Dine Brands recently adopted a poison pill to block a takeover bid from investment firms Arkhouse Management and Cobblers Cove Capital.

articles.title_orig: 2026 iPad mini review: Maximizing the mini
articles.title_zh: 2026 iPad mini review: Maximizing the mini
articles.content_orig:
The iPad mini has long felt like a niche product. It has earned a reputation as a quality tablet for people who want something small, comfortable, and portable, but its small screen and comparatively limited processing power have restricted its appeal, making it best suited to watching media or playing games.
With the 2026 version , the iPad mini is more competitive than ever. Its chip is current, its speakers are better, and, most impressively, it trades its 8.3-inch IPS screen for an 8.5-inch OLED that can hold its own against other premium tablets. There isn’t much more you can ask of an iPad this small.
But at just $50 less than the larger, more powerful iPad Air (11-inch) , the iPad mini still has a hard time making a case for itself.
The most immediately noticeable change to the 2026 iPad mini is its display. At 0.2 inches larger than the 2024 iPad mini’s screen, the difference might not sound like much, but it has a meaningful impact on a tablet this small. Beyond providing a bigger view of photos, video content, and lengthy documents, the extra space makes it easier to work with multiple windows, giving you more room to view them and adjust their size and location.
One of our biggest complaints about the prior mini was its bezels, which felt large for a tablet of its size. This time, Apple managed to fit a larger screen in a slightly smaller tablet (7.69 × 5.22 × 0.21 inches and 0.56 pounds for the 2026 mini versus 7.69 × 5.3 × 0.25 inches and 0.65 pounds for the 2024 mini) by reducing the bezels by 24 percent. The result is a streamlined viewing experience that feels more modern and appropriate for a new Apple product.
And you’ll certainly want to watch content on the 2316 × 1512 OLED display, which packs 326 pixels per inch. OLED displays often lack the brightness of their LCD-LED counterparts, but the gap has narrowed in recent years. The new mini is brighter than its IPS-based predecessor, with Apple claiming full-screen brightness of up to 600 nits, compared to 500 nits on the previous model. It’s also much better suited to HDR content, with peak HDR brightness reaching 1,200 nits for highlights and a contrast ratio of 2,000,000:1.
Since content consumption is arguably the mini’s strongest use case, it makes sense for Apple to focus on changes that enhance the viewing experience. Watching shows and movies feels as luxurious as possible on a screen this size, and the mini maximizes its display in nearly all the ways that matter.
I say “nearly” because the mini still has a 60 Hz refresh rate; 120Hz is limited to the iPad Pro . A 120 Hz refresh rate makes little difference when watching most shows or movies, but it can make some tasks, such as scrolling through long documents, look smoother. Still, the difference is less noticeable on a smaller screen.
Overall, the refresh rate didn’t feel like a drawback during regular use. Apple has gone a step further , noting that OLEDs typically have faster response times than IPS displays. That’s generally true when discussing gray-to-gray (GtG) response times. However, moving picture response time (MPRT) can be a better indicator of potential persistence-related motion blur, including during scrolling, because it measures how long an image remains visible on the display, contributing to blur as your eyes track moving content. GtG, by contrast, measures how quickly individual pixels transition between shades. Slower pixel transitions can create motion artifacts such as ghosting.
According to Blur Busters’ MPRT Indicator , the mini has an MPRT of about 17 ms, about what I’d expect from a 60 Hz IPS display. Anyone who needs a high-refresh screen will still want to look at the Pro series.
One feature the mini borrows from the iPad Pro but that other iPads lack is the option for nano-texture glass, which is designed to reduce glare. It costs an extra $100 and is only available on the 256GB and 512GB versions of the mini.
The 2024 mini debuted with a year-old chip, but this year’s model sports Apple’s latest mobile processor. The 2026 mini makes a considerable jump from the A17 Pro, a 3-nanometer, iPhone 15 Pro-era chip from 2023, to the A20 Pro, a 2-nanometer chip that debuted in the new iPhone 18 Pro .
The newer chip has 50 percent more memory bandwidth, which significantly boosts graphics performance. It’s also up to 60 percent faster.
I tested the 512GB version of the iPad Mini, which, like the 128GB and 256GB versions, features a seven-core integrated GPU. The 512GB model, however, gets a bump from five CPU cores to six and doubles the number of 16-core Neural Engines from one to two, promising better performance in on-device AI applications, such as image generation.
I don’t expect many people to run particularly intensive workloads on a tablet this small. Still, tasks such as photo editing, light video editing, and juggling many open applications felt smooth. The performance boost makes the iPad mini much more powerful than the standard iPad 11 , which uses an A16 processor. The iPad Pro (M5) and the iPad Air (M4), however, remain better equipped for demanding workloads such as video editing and 3D rendering.
Siri AI is still in beta, so we won’t cover that in this review. But the tablet supports features under the Apple Intelligence umbrella, including various generative AI capabilities. Tasks like removing objects from photos, changing a photo’s perspective, or extending a photo’s borders should take roughly the same amount of time on the 512GB iPad mini as they do on the iPhone 18 Pro. In my experience, that’s usually about 20 seconds.
The mini is surprisingly loud. Its speakers are powerful enough to make TV dialogue easy to hear, even with my noisy heater running in the background.
The tablet has two woofers designed to deliver higher volume and stronger bass than the prior mini. A pair of custom-designed tweeters between the tablet’s glass and aluminum enclosure are intended to improve the clarity of higher frequencies.
You won’t get the deepest bass or the crispest high notes, but the speakers surpassed my expectations when playing music. I didn’t immediately feel the need to connect the iPad to dedicated speakers.
And the mini pulls this off without any visible speaker holes in its chassis.
That detail helped the mini earn the first IP67 rating for an iPad. The Ingress Protection rating means the device is “dust-tight” and “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water,” according to the International Electrotechnical Commission .
The 2026 mini has the same 12 MP front and back cameras as its 2024 predecessor, but the front-facing camera has moved from one of the shorter sides to one of the longer sides. This took some getting used to for FaceTiming and selfies. Holding the tablet in portrait orientation now places you off-center in the frame, while holding it in landscape mode to FaceTime on the go quickly became uncomfortable. The new location was fine when I could sit down and prop the tablet on a stand.
Another addition is the back camera’s Adaptive True Tone flash, which Apple markets as a way to quickly scan documents. When the Camera app identifies a document, such as a piece of paper or a book, it automatically adjusts which of the camera’s LEDs light up to minimize shadows and produce clearer text.
When I used the tablet’s camera to photograph text on both a piece of paper and a book, it quickly used machine learning to identify them as documents. A pop-up appeared, offering the option to “Scan Document”; selecting it allowed me to automatically take a picture of just the document. It’s not a feature many people will use regularly, but when the need arises, it makes capturing a sharp, detailed image of text considerably easier.

articles.title_orig: Putin will not attend Britain's G20 summit, UK PM Burnham says
articles.title_zh: Putin will not attend Britain's G20 summit, UK PM Burnham says
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Vladimir Putin is not invited to the G20 summit in Manchester.
Asked whether the Russian president would be invited to the annual meeting, which the UK is hosting in November 2027, Burnham said "no" because of sanctions against the Kremlin.
The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
But US president Donald Trump has sparked controversy by inviting Putin to this year's G20, which he will host in Miami in December. The Kremlin has not yet said whether Putin will attend.
Russia is a member of the G20 - a group of 19 nations, the European Union and African Union - while Ukraine is not, but the ongoing war in Ukraine has loomed large over recent summits.
Putin has not attended any major global summit since he launched his invasion and ongoing war in Ukraine.
Asked about inviting him to the G20 in Manchester in 2027, Burnham told The Economist he "will not be coming because of an outstanding sanction" on senior Russian figures.
He said the meeting would provide "a real opportunity" to work with Chinese president Xi Jinping on safety regulations for artificial intelligence (AI).
Pressed on whether the UK could bring the US and China around the same table to agree on global AI supervision, Burnham said: "As I sit here today, that feels challenging, but we've got to hold out the need to find global agreements on AI.
"If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify.
"So you've got to go into it with that aim."
He stressed the need "to find global agreements on AI," adding: "If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify. So you've got to go into it with that aim."
His decision not to include Putin in next year's gathering in Manchester comes after European diplomats refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in October.
The so-called "family photo" would usually include representatives from all nations in attendance, but this year it was cancelled.
The US decision to invite Lavrov in the first place - which itself came after further public rows between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky - also attracted criticism.
Discussing Ukraine, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told Lavrov at the summit: "Let me say this directly to the Russian foreign minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is."
The UK last hosted the G20 summit in 2009. Next year's two-day event will take place in the Manchester Central Convention Centre in Manchester city centre and host thousands of diplomats and delegates, as well as world leaders.
The government has said it will use its G20 presidency in 2027 to "reinforce global economic stability" and "benefit people in every part of the UK".

articles.content_orig:
Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.
Discord is moving its apps fully over to the Rust programming language.
Discord is finally giving up on Electron, the cross-platform framework that lets developers build desktop apps using web technologies. Electron web apps are notoriously heavy on system resources, and Discord is now moving its desktop app fully to Rust — a modern programming language designed for speed and memory safety.
“We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there,” explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X . “That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust.”
Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app.
It’s not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company “hope to get it into testing with users soon.”

articles.title_zh: Finnish court jails captain and crew member for 'aggravated criminal damage' over Baltic cable sabotage
articles.content_orig:
A Finnish court on Thursday convicted the Russian captain and a senior crew member of the cargo ship Fitburg for damaging two undersea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland last year.
The Helsinki District Court found the two defendants guilty of "aggravated criminal damage."
It said in a statement that they had intentionally dragged the ship's anchor along the seabed for around 130 kilometers (81 miles).
The captain was sentenced to three and a half years in jail, while the crew member, an Azerbaijani citizen, was sentenced to two years and 10 months.
They were also ordered to jointly pay around €1.9 million ($2.1 million) in damages, the Reuters news agency reported, with the captain to pay about €85,000 more.
The defendants denied any wrongdoing and have challenged Finland's jurisdiction in the case.
Finnish authorities seized the vessel on December 31 on suspicion that it had damaged cables linking Finland 's capital, Helsinki, and Tallinn, Estonia.
Finnish police at the time said the ship had been dragging its anchor for hours when it was discovered in Finland's exclusive economic zone.
The Fitburg and its 14-member crew had been en route to the port of Haifa, Israel, from the Russian city of St. Petersburg when the incident occurred.
Finland has stepped up efforts to protect its undersea infrastructure following a series of incidents involving cables and pipelines in the Baltic Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI lays out new policy framework for data centers
articles.title_zh: OpenAI lays out new policy framework for data centers
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday, two days after voters at the polls roundly rejected the rapid expansion of AI.
The artificial intelligence company said in its commitments that for data centers it owns and operates, it will solicit community input, publish construction plans and stay away from using non-disclosure agreements with public officials. Additionally, in a policy blueprint, OpenAI encouraged policymakers to enact similar commitments as laws.
"What we're doing with this blueprint is really laying out the best lessons that we have learned and committing to applying them as they go forward," OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane told reporters during a Wednesday briefing. "This will help ensure that there is a very high floor in terms of how people move forward."
Other tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic , have outlined several similar commitments .
On Tuesday, Americans issued a stinging rebuke of data centers at the polls. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures for all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday.
Opposition to AI data centers mounted swiftly over the summer across both sides of the political aisle. Consumers grappling with inflation, rising grocery prices and stubbornly high prices at the pump grew worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, they became a physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy and anxiety around AI.
AI companies like OpenAI depend on AI data centers to serve customers and develop new models, and they're seeking to build out as rapidly as possible to meet demand. In February, OpenAI told investors that it's targeting $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and the company has since announced massive data center projects in Georgia and Ohio .
OpenAI has repeatedly pledged to protect ratepayers and invest in local communities this year, and Lehane said the company's latest commitments build on many of its previous initiatives. He said the policy blueprint has been in the works since August, and that he met with dozens of lawmakers and candidates since then.
"Having these conversations now actually helps put more energy into the momentum, so that when people come back in late January, new Congress is in in session, a lot of the work is being done in advance," Lehane said.

articles.title_orig: China threatens retaliation as EU mulls trade “kill-switch”
articles.title_zh: China threatens retaliation as EU mulls trade “kill-switch”
articles.content_orig:
China’s ambassador to the EU, Cai Run, threatened on Thursday to retaliate if the EU adopted unilateral measures against Chinese interests.
The statement came as the European Commission is working on a new trade defence tool, dubbed a “kill-switch,” that could cut off Chinese access to the EU market in the event of serious market disruption caused by its aggressive trade policies.
“China opposes politicising economic and trade issues, overstretching the concept of security, and resorting to unilateral or maximum pressure,” Cai said.
He added: “If the EU side insists on adopting restrictive and discriminatory measures against China, China will have to take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its interests.”
As the EU faces a record-high trade deficit with China of €1 billion a day, Brussels is seeking to protect its market from low-cost Chinese imports, which have surged by 25% over the past year, according to Chinese customs.
Last October, EU leaders tasked the European Commission with developing an instrument that could be rapidly deployed against countries whose political or economic actions have serious repercussions for the EU market.
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič told MEPs on Wednesday that the tool should be presented by the end of the year and would allow the EU “to react much faster, even by limiting the exports into the European Union.” He added that it would target “countries which are treating us [the EU] unfairly or which are harming European interests.”
Presented as country-agnostic, the tool would nevertheless directly target Chinese interests, which rely heavily on the EU’s 450 million consumers to sell their excess of production.
France and Germany pushed for such an instrument in early October, as every EU member state now faces a trade deficit with Beijing, with Chinese imports threatening entire sectors of their industries.
The Franco-German move came amid ongoing negotiations between Brussels and Beijing, which had begun the previous June with the aim of rebalancing trade relations. It also came just days before the Commission reached a deal on 9 October to reduce Chinese imports of hybrid cars into the EU.
Since the deal on cars, talks have resumed at a technical level between EU and Chinese officials, with Brussels hoping to replicate such an agreement in other sectors. A new meeting between Šefčovič and China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao is scheduled for March 2027.
Given the urgency of the situation, EU leaders have also asked the Commission to adopt measures, including quotas and tariffs, against Chinese imports in the chemicals and machinery industries, as pressure on the EU market has become unsustainable for European producers.
Šefčovič has repeatedly said that, with thousands of jobs at stake in the EU, the EU-China trade issue had become a political one in Europe, with high expectations among EU citizens.
Despite ongoing talks with China since June, the Commission has continued to impose additional duties on Chinese imports entering the EU following investigations product by product that found Chinese producers were benefiting from unfair pricing or subsidies from China.
This is not the first time China has threatened the EU with countermeasures. It already did so against a bill – the Industrial Accelerator Act - currently under discussion by the EU’s co-legislators seeking to limit access to EU public procurement and impose strict conditions on investments in the EU market, also targeting Beijing without explicitly naming it.

Two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Thursday, as Iran continues to report a growing number of incidents with vessels trying to transit the Strait on routes unauthorized by the Islamic Republic.
One of the oil tankers hit a naval mine while it was attempting to move south of the Strait. Another tanker caught fire as it was on its way out in the eastern part of the Strait, and a tugboat that had approached it to help also caught fire, according to Iran’s elite force.
Separately, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which is affiliated with the Royal Navy, said on Thursday that it had received a report of an incident 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar, in which a tanker has been struck by two unidentified projectiles. articles.title_orig: How the midterms could fuel the K-shaped AI trade
articles.title_zh: How the midterms could fuel the K-shaped AI trade
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. midterms could widen the AI divide: tighter data center rules may reward tech giants with capacity in hand and squeeze debt-funded companies trying to catch up.
Democratic victories in key gubernatorial races raised the prospect of tougher scrutiny for data center projects, adding to investor concerns about how quickly new capacity can be built and financed.
In Texas, Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a statewide moratorium on new data center permits, although projects already under construction would reportedly be exempt.
As the markets digested the results on Wednesday, Microsoft and Amazon each surged more than 6%, while AI infrastructure provider CoreWeave plunged around 10%. Chipmakers Micron and Nvidia fell 7% and 3.17%, respectively.
Differences in borrowing costs are playing a key role in the split, James Sullivan, managing director and co-head of global fundamental research at JPMorgan, told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia " on Thursday.
Sullivan said borrowing spreads have widened significantly for neocloud companies, leaving their cost of additional capital substantially higher than that of hyperscalers that benefit from more diversified customers and revenue streams.
"The fact that you're seeing this bifurcation in equity performance is largely driven by the view that existing capacity is significantly more valuable now because of incremental supply constraints," he said.
The midterm results could reinforce that view if they make new projects more vulnerable to permitting delays.
BMI warned that a sharp slowdown in data center construction and AI investment could produce a greater-than-expected decline in overall investment, The Business Times reported, citing the firm's post-midterm analysis.
The potential impact is uneven across the construction pipeline. Much of the data center capacity expected to come online in 2027 is already under construction, limiting the near-term impact of new restrictions.
Projects planned for 2028 face greater exposure to permitting delays and regulatory uncertainty, investment bank Nomura said in a note Wednesday about the midterm results.
Tighter regulations on data center construction could become a more significant headwind to AI investment from 2028, the firm said.
Shares of Nvidia-backed neocloud CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren fell at least 30% in October, as tightening credit markets raised questions about how AI infrastructure projects would be financed . CoreWeave's five-year credit default swap spread has surged past 1,100 basis points, reflecting rising costs for investors seeking protection against a potential default.
The distinction may be how well companies can absorb delays and fund the capacity they do build. Hyperscalers have broader cloud businesses and more internally generated cash flow, while lower-rated neoclouds face greater exposure to borrowing costs, energy prices and refinancing conditions, JPMorgan Asset Management said in an Oct. 20 research note.
The asset manager said financially stronger hyperscalers could also secure cheaper capacity or acquire assets if weaker operators scale back.

By ANGHARAD CARRICK, BUSINESS NEWS EDITOR
Updated: 07:08 EDT, 5 November 2026
The Bank of England raised interest rates to 4 per cent in a blow to borrowers already battling higher mortgage and energy costs.
Eight members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted to increase by a quarter of a point, while Catherine Mann voted to raise by 0.5 per cent.
It is the first time the bank has increased borrowing costs since August 2023, as it seeks to tame surging inflation driven by higher energy costs and the conflict in the Middle East.
Economists and traders had expected the rate hike after September’s inflation reading reached 3.5 per cent, its highest level in 11 months and well above the Bank’s 2 per cent target.
The BoE hopes that making borrowing more expensive will help to dampen demand and act as a drag on spending and investment, keeping inflation in check which it now expects to rise to 5 per cent by the middle of 2027.
The Iran war has gone on for longer than anticipated, and the BoE is now playing catch-up with other central banks, including the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank, which have already raised rates this year.
The Bank adopted a ‘wait and see’ approach in the immediate months after the outbreak of the conflict, with hopes that higher gilt yields - which rose to multi-decade highs last month and have dragged mortgage rates higher - would do the brunt work.
But with the conflict now in its ninth month, there are concerns that higher inflation could become embedded in the economy.
The Bank of England raised base rate to 4%, the first increase in over three years
Economists are split on whether today’s decision marks the start of a series of rate hikes.
Much will depend on whether the US and Iran can broker a peace deal, which would alleviate some of the pressure on the BoE to act again.
Kallum Pickering, chief economist at Peel Hunt, said there is ‘little evidence nor reason to believe this will turn into a persistent inflation shock.’
He added: ‘BoE policymakers do not want to repeat the 2022 experience when they fell behind the curve in curbing an inflation surge which they had initially described as ‘transitory’.
Assuming that energy prices fall back next year, any 'second-round' effects would be muted, said Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics.
This means this week's meeting is unlikely to mark the start of a series of rate hikes, he said, expecting policymakers to start cutting interest rates in late 2027 and into 2028.
Deutsche Bank and Morgan Stanley disagree, forecasting another rate rise in February to bring the base rate to 4.25 per cent.
Governor Andrew Bailey indicated that the Bank would make 'adjust Bank Rate as necessary to ensure CPI inflation returns to the 2 per cent target in the medium term.'
In the immediate term, today’s decision will pile further pressure on homeowners who will see their mortgage rates rise further, with some economists predicting more pain into next year.
Figures from UK Finance show the rate hike will add £30.72 a month to the average tracker repayment, and £14.28 to the variable rate.
And inflation, already above the Bank's 2 per cent target, is expected to rise even further this winter as Ofgem's price cap is forecast to rise by around 25 per cent in January 2027.
The latest figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility, released alongside the Budget last week, show inflation climbing to nearly 4 per cent at the start of 2027. The Bank of England expects it to increase to 5 per cent by the middle of the year.

The Joint List alliance of Arab-led parties says it will back Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a new government after last week’s election.
“The Joint List announced today, Thursday, that it will inform the President of the State, Isaac Herzog, this evening of its decision to recommend that Gadi Eisenkot be tasked with forming the government,” the alliance said in a statement.
Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in Israel’s 120-seat parliament in last week’s general election, a result that could give them significant influence over the formation of the next government.
Once the Joint List’s 11 lawmakers formally submit their recommendation, Eisenkot is expected to have the backing of 67 lawmakers, exceeding the 61-seat majority threshold in the Knesset.
Earlier, Ra’am, an Arab-led party with eight seats, said it would also recommend Eisenkot.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc with 53 seats may not yield 53 endorsements, as Degel HaTorah, which holds four of United Torah Judaism’s seven seats, said it would recommend neither candidate.
The ultra-Orthodox faction broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting Haredi men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has accepted the certified results of last week’s parliamentary elections and begun consultations with party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.
On Wednesday, the president said he had met representatives of the Religious Zionism and Zehut, Shas, and Yisrael Beytenu factions.
He “received their recommendations regarding the identity of the Knesset member upon whom the task of forming the government should be assigned”, Herzog said on X.
Herzog added that talks would also continue on Thursday.
Once the consultations end, Herzog will choose the candidate he considers best placed to assemble a coalition, almost certainly Netanyahu or Eisenkot. He has several days to announce his decision, after which the nominee will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
If neither man succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year.
